title: Wives for Benjamin, and No King in Israel
summary: Having sworn not to give their daughters to Benjamin, the Israelites grieve that a tribe is about to disappear. They destroy Jabesh-gilead, which had not come to the assembly, and give its four hundred virgins to the surviving Benjamites. When there are not enough, they tell the remaining men to seize wives from the young women dancing at the yearly feast at Shiloh, and the book closes with its refrain that there was no king and everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
story: Chapter 20 ended with Benjamin reduced to six hundred men hiding at the rock of Rimmon. Chapter 21 shows Israel trying to undo the damage it has done, and making things worse. A rash oath, like Jephthah's in chapter 11, traps the people, and their solution is more violence against their own: the destruction of a town and the abduction of women. The book that opened with Israel asking the LORD who should go up first against the Canaanites (1:1) ends with Israel devising schemes on its own to repair the damage of a civil war. The final verse repeats the refrain of the epilogue and sends the reader on to Ruth, set in the same period, and to 1 Samuel, where Israel will ask for a king.
historical:
Jabesh-gilead lay east of the Jordan, in Gilead. It had strong ties with Benjamin, and those ties appear again later: when the Ammonites threatened Jabesh-gilead, Saul the Benjamite rescued it (1 Samuel 11), and after Saul's death its men recovered his body from the Philistines and buried it (1 Samuel 31:11-13). Some interpreters think the story in this chapter explains that bond, since many Benjamites would have been descended from the women of Jabesh-gilead.

Shiloh, in the hill country of Ephraim, was the site of the tabernacle for much of the period of the judges (18:31; Joshua 18:1). The detailed directions to it in 21:19 (north of Bethel, east of the road to Shechem, south of Lebonah) have puzzled readers, since Shiloh would have been well known; some think they reflect a time when the site had been destroyed and was less familiar. The yearly feast there may be the same as the annual pilgrimage in 1 Samuel 1:3, and the dancing in the vineyards suggests a harvest festival, perhaps the Feast of Tabernacles or a local vintage celebration.
cultural:
Oaths sworn before God were regarded as binding, even when made rashly, which is why Israel does not simply cancel its vow. The law allowed some vows to be annulled (Numbers 30), but an oath taken by the whole assembly was treated with great seriousness. The Israelites also swore a second oath, that anyone who failed to come to Mizpah would be put to death. They use that second oath to justify the attack on Jabesh-gilead.

The herem, or devotion to destruction, was a practice of the conquest in which a city and its inhabitants were given over to God by total destruction. Here Israel applies it to one of its own towns, and sparing the virgins shows that the purpose was not devotion to God but securing wives. The abduction at Shiloh follows a form of marriage by capture known in the ancient world, but Israel's law provided no such arrangement for its own people. The elders' plan to tell the fathers that they had not really given their daughters, and so had not broken the oath, keeps the letter of the vow while ignoring its spirit.
literary: The chapter mirrors the book's opening. Judges began with Israel asking the LORD's direction and ends with Israel making its own plans. The people weep and ask why this has happened (21:3), but no answer from the LORD is recorded, and the people act on their own. The repetition of the phrase no one had come (21:8-9) and the note that there were not enough women (21:14) move the plot to its second scheme. The narrator's flat tone in describing the abduction lets the reader feel its wrongness. The last verse, “In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (21:25), repeats 17:6 exactly and frames the whole epilogue. It serves as the book's closing verdict.

outline.t: Israel grieves over Benjamin and its oath
Jabesh-gilead destroyed and four hundred virgins taken
Peace with Benjamin, and not enough wives
The plan to seize the daughters of Shiloh
All return home; no king in Israel

doctrines.note: Israel tries to repair the damage of one sin by committing others. The chapter shows how sin compounds when people rely on their own schemes instead of seeking God and repenting.

The book ends by naming Israel's need: a king who would lead the people in faithfulness. The rest of the Old Testament traces the rise of that kingship, and its failures, until the coming of the true king.

Israel grieves that a tribe is missing because the covenant made the twelve tribes one people. Even in its disorder, Israel recognized that it was incomplete without Benjamin, which shows the covenant's lasting claim.

words.note: Shava, to swear an oath. The chapter turns on two oaths, one against giving daughters to Benjamin and one against those who stayed away from the assembly. The Israelites treat their oaths as binding while inventing ways around them, and the whole plot shows the danger of vows made in anger.

Charam, to devote to destruction, used in 21:11. The word belongs to the conquest's language of devoting a city wholly to God. Its use against an Israelite town, with some women spared as wives, shows how far Israel had drifted from the covenant's purposes.

Perets, breach or gap. In 21:15 the people say the LORD has made a breach in the tribes of Israel. The word is used of a break in a wall. Israel recognizes the loss of Benjamin as a gap in the people of God, though its attempts to fill it cause further harm.

Nacham, to be sorry or to grieve. The Israelites grieve over Benjamin in 21:6 and 21:15. The word can mean to comfort, to regret, or to change one's mind. Israel's grief is real, but it leads to schemes rather than repentance.

christ: Judges ends with the longing that runs through its final chapters: for a king who would lead Israel in doing what is right in God's eyes rather than their own. The next books answer in part. Ruth, set in the same period, ends with the name of David, and 1 Samuel tells of David's rise. But David's line also failed, and the prophets looked for a king from his line who would reign with justice and righteousness (Isaiah 9:6-7; Jeremiah 23:5-6). The New Testament proclaims Jesus as that king. The chapter itself does not predict him; it shows why he was needed. The breach in Israel's tribes, and the violence against women used to repair it, show a people unable to heal themselves, and the gospel speaks of a king who restores what is broken without harming the vulnerable.

hard.q: How can the Bible end a book with a mass killing and the abduction of women, with no comment from God?
hard.a: The ending is deliberately unsettling. Judges does not present these events as models but as evidence of what Israel had become. The narrator's final verse is the book's verdict: this is what happens when there is no king and everyone does what is right in his own eyes. The absence of any word from the LORD after the people's question in 21:3 is itself significant, since Israel seems to have stopped seeking him. Interpreters differ on the tone of the ending. Some read it as a call for monarchy, looking ahead to David; others see it as a picture of a people who have lost their way so completely that only God's own intervention could restore them. Either way, the reader is meant to be troubled, and the fact that Scripture records these acts without softening them is part of its honesty about human sin, including the sin of God's people.

questions: Israel kept the letter of its oath while finding ways around its spirit. Where are you tempted to keep rules in form while ignoring their purpose?
Israel grieved over Benjamin but tried to solve the problem without seeking God. How can grief lead to wisdom rather than to more harm?
Judges ends with everyone doing what was right in his own eyes. What would it look like for your community to seek what is right in God's eyes instead?
